title: next surfaces an open arc root whose members are still open — make rollup structural
body:
Reported from agent fleets on Y and FactoryGame: a root filed with trk in / add --in appears on trk next while its members are open, because next only consults needs edges and never checks isArc on the candidate itself. Eight hand-repaired rollup edges accumulated in under a week.

Agreed direction (pending design discussion): fix eligibility in Store.next — an open task that isArc is eligible only when no direct non-parked member fails satisfiesPrereq (vacuously eligible when all members are parked; do NOT reuse arcComplete, which returns false for that case). Do the same in render so the projection agrees.

Rejected: auto-creating root-needs-member edges at authoring time — cycle risk with arc-as-prereq (EXIT-threshold pattern: E needs arc A, member M needs E, auto-edge A->M closes the cycle), log noise, needs a paired auto-undep, and does not repair existing trackers.

title: show --body: raw body read path for safe edit round-trips
body: trk show indents the body for display and there was no raw accessor, so editing a body meant parsing log.jsonl by hand or round-tripping indented display output (caused the 0d2 body corruption). Added: trk show <id> --body prints the body verbatim, making trk edit <id> --body "$(trk show <id> --body)" lossless.

title: doc unset: tombstone a doc_id -> path registration
body: No way to unregister a doc mapping (ProgramPassAudit -> blank). Added: trk doc unset <doc_id> emits setDocPath with an empty path; the fold removes the mapping (resolve fails, list hides, render falls back to the raw doc_id), serializeState never emits removed entries so compact GCs the tombstone. Idempotent like untag/undep; a later set revives (last-write-wins).

Reported from agent fleets on Y and FactoryGame: a root filed with trk in / add --in appears on trk next while its members are open, because next only consults needs edges and never checks isArc on the candidate itself. Eight hand-repaired rollup edges accumulated in under a week.

Agreed direction (pending design discussion): fix eligibility in Store.next — an open task that isArc is eligible only when no direct non-parked member fails satisfiesPrereq (vacuously eligible when all members are parked; do NOT reuse arcComplete, which returns false for that case). Do the same in render so the projection agrees.

Rejected: auto-creating root-needs-member edges at authoring time — cycle risk with arc-as-prereq (EXIT-threshold pattern: E needs arc A, member M needs E, auto-edge A->M closes the cycle), log noise, needs a paired auto-undep, and does not repair existing trackers.

Fixed via the drained-vs-complete ruling (2026-07-13), red-teamed before landing. An arc root is a container: Store.next holds an open root back until the arc is drained (arcDrained: no direct non-parked member unsatisfied; vacuously drained when all members are parked), then surfaces it once as the close-out prompt. The arc-as-prereq special case was deleted: a needs edge targeting a root gates on the root's own state — the explicit completion judgment — so closing the root is what unblocks dependents. Rejected: authoring-time derived root-needs-member edges (union-merge can forge a cycle that bricks the store; ignores parked; irreversible) and a done-when-complete auto-close field (conflates the observable drained fact with the completion judgment; auto-done + archive graduates a still-growing arc into an immutable tombstone). Full rationale in docs/design.md.

title: Default priority should be a HIGH positive number, not 0 — today any explicit priority SINKS a task

body:
Filed 2026-08-06 from Enix (Scott). Priority is documented 'int, lower first' and defaults to 0 (model.zig:85 'priority: i32 = 0'; json_codec.zig:419 getIntDefault(obj,'priority',0)).

THE DEFECT: because the default is 0 and ordering is lower-first, the default is already the HIGHEST priority. Any explicit priority a user sets is a positive int, which sorts BELOW every untouched task. Setting a task 'high priority' therefore does the opposite of what the user intends, silently. Measured in the Enix backlog 2026-08-06: 257 of 259 open tasks sit at the default 0, so 'trk edit <id> --priority 10' buries a task beneath 257 others. The only way to raise something today is a NEGATIVE number, which no part of the CLI or docs suggests.

CANDIDATE SHAPES, not chosen here:
 (1) Change the default to a high positive constant (say 100 or 1000). Clean going forward, but it does NOT migrate stored values: every existing task keeps a literal 0 and would outrank every new default-priority task -- the same inversion, with the sign flipped. Needs a migration event or a one-time rewrite.
 (2) MIGRATION-FREE VARIANT, probably better: keep 0 as the stored 'unset' sentinel and treat it AS the default when ORDERING -- i.e. sort key = (priority == 0 ? DEFAULT : priority). store.zig:1031 already treats 0 as unset for rendering ('if (t.priority != 0)'), so the sentinel reading is established in the codebase rather than invented here. No stored data changes, no migration, and an explicit priority immediately means what a user expects in both directions.
 (3) Reject 0 as an explicit value so the sentinel can never be ambiguous.

Whichever is taken, --help should state the direction and the default explicitly: today it says only 'Priority: int, lower first', which is true and still leads a reader to exactly the wrong action.

Pairs with the sibling task on next()'s ranking -- together they are why priority is close to inert today.

title: next(): a task's own priority can never beat arc-seq, and arcless tasks sort last via a maxInt sentinel — so a high-priority arcless task is buried

body:
Filed 2026-08-06 from Enix (Scott): 'return arcless high priority tasks in next'.

WHAT THE CODE DOES (store.zig:1507-1517, 1528-1583, read at 389bfe5):
  Ranked.less compares best_arc_seq FIRST and uses priority only as a TIEBREAK:
      if (x.best_arc_seq != y.best_arc_seq) return x.best_arc_seq < y.best_arc_seq;
      if (x.priority != y.priority) return x.priority < y.priority;
  and best_arc_seq is initialised to maxInt(i64) with the comment 'sentinel: arc-less sorts last'.

TWO CONSEQUENCES, both surprising:
 1. ARCLESS TASKS ARE BURIED REGARDLESS OF PRIORITY. They do appear in next (the doc comment is right that they are not excluded), but the maxInt sentinel puts every one of them below every arc-member, so no priority however extreme can lift one. A user who files an urgent standalone task and sets it high priority sees no change at all.
 2. PRIORITY IS NEARLY VESTIGIAL EVEN INSIDE AN ARC. best_arc_seq is the task's SEQ WITHIN ITS ARC, not the arc's priority, so priority only ever separates tasks that share an identical seq. Verified empirically from Enix: a probe added with --in <arc> (default seq) and --priority -50 jumped to the top of next, because it TIED on seq and won the tiebreak -- not because priority outranked anything.

WANTED: a task's own priority should be able to compete, so an arcless high-priority task surfaces. Shapes worth weighing (not chosen): make priority the PRIMARY key with arc-seq as the tiebreak; or keep arc-seq primary but let a priority below some threshold escape the arcless sentinel; or drop the maxInt sentinel and give arcless tasks a neutral rank so priority decides. The first is simplest to reason about but changes ordering for every existing consumer -- Enix's own frontier included -- so it wants a deliberate call, not a quiet swap.

Pairs with the sibling task on the priority DEFAULT. Together they explain why priority is close to inert today: the default is already the strongest value, and the field is a tiebreak behind a key most users never set.
